text: His name was Shah Jahan, and under him the Mughal Empire reached the peak of its wealth
and its show.
He sat on the peacock throne, made of gold and covered in jewels, and said into it was
a diamond the size of a small egg, the Kohinoor, the mountain of light.
Remember the diamond from the beginning?
This is where its journey starts.
In this age, India was one of the richest places on earth, and the secret wasn't diamonds,
it was cloth.
Remember the cotton from the Indus?
Indian cotton now dressed people from Japan to Africa to London.
Silver poured in from Europe and the Americas to pay for it.
When Shah Jahan's favorite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their 14th child, he
built her a tomb on the river at Agra.
Around 20,000 workers and craftsmen. More than 20 years. White marble from Rajasthan, inlaid with stones from across Asia.
The Taj Mahal.
Now, let's bust a myth. You've probably heard that once it was finished, Shah Jahan cut off the builder's hands so they could never build anything as beautiful again.
There's no evidence for it. No record from the time mentions it. It's a much later legend.
But Shah Jahan's ending was dark enough without it.
His four sons fought a brutal war for the throne.
The winner was Aurangzeb.
Aurangzeb had his brothers killed and locked his own father inside the fort at Agra.
From its windows, Shah Jahan could see the Taj across the river.
Your dinner, Majesty. Is my son coming to visit? He sends...his regards. Regards.
I gave him an empire. Aurangzeb ruled for nearly 50 years and pushed the empire to its
largest size ever. But he spent his last 25 years at war in the south, and he brought
back the jizya tax. His toughest enemy was a young Maratha leader from the hills near
Pune, Shivaji, a master of fast raids and hill forts.
Placed under house arrest in Agra, he escaped, as the famous story goes, hidden inside giant
baskets of sweets.
After Aurangzeb died in 1707, the empire cracked.
Governors became kings, the Marathas spread across the center of India, and in 1739,
the Persian ruler Nader Shah marched in and sacked Delhi. He carried home the peacock throne and
the Kohinoor. Remember Mahmoud's camels? India's treasure was leaving again.
But the next visitors weren't interested in thrones. They didn't come with armies. They came with account books.
